telos.statement: Determine whether the proposed diagnostic reasoning framework Truth → Perception → Action → Ownership → Effect is a sound, discriminating, and decision-useful way to diagnose product failures in Decision Lab, or whether it collapses distinct constructs, mixes levels of analysis, omits material mechanisms, or should be represented in a different structure.
telos.success_condition: Return a bounded decision about whether to USE_EXISTING, ADAPT, TEST, or RETIRE the five-part framework; identify the smallest set of distinctions that actually changes diagnosis and intervention choice; name the strongest competing decomposition; specify what can be resolved conceptually now versus what requires FIELD evidence; and produce a falsifiable next move rather than a prettier taxonomy.

current_state.summary: A product-analysis reasoning chain was proposed during review of Decision Lab: Reality → Model → Representation → Interpretation → Action → Learning. From it, five diagnostic questions were derived: (1) Truth — what does the system actually know? (2) Perception — what does the user think the system knows? (3) Action — what should the user do next with that state? (4) Ownership — can the user carry the distinction/judgment themselves rather than merely follow the system, especially where transfer matters? (5) Effect — did the resulting action actually change the target behavior/outcome? The current intuition is that these five questions correspond to distinct failure classes: instrument/research failure, representation failure, interaction/journey failure, learning/transfer failure, and intervention-effect failure. Motivation was deliberately not made a primitive because it may be an outcome produced by several of these mechanisms. Ownership was acknowledged as product-specific rather than universal. The framework was generated analytically from a causal chain, not validated against a corpus of product failures. The live question is whether this is a genuinely useful decomposition or merely a compelling verbal compression.
known_constraints: Do not promote a memorable five-part list into a canonical method merely because it sounds coherent.
Do not force MECE if the underlying system is causal, recursive, or has moderators rather than serial stages.
Separate epistemic state, user perception, action selection, behavior execution, learning/transfer, and downstream outcome if they are not the same construct.
Ownership may be a moderator, mechanism, or product-specific requirement rather than a universal stage; test that rather than assuming it.
Action clarity is not identical to action execution; motivation, ability, opportunity, trust, cost and expected value may intervene.
Effect may exist at several levels: immediate behavior, transfer, retention, skill change, external outcome. Do not collapse them.
The framework should be judged by discrimination power: does locating a failure in one component lead to a materially different next intervention or evidence request?
A useful framework should survive neighboring cases outside Decision Lab; a framework that only redescribes this one product should not be called general.
Prefer the smallest reversible test or comparison that can determine whether the framework improves diagnosis over an ordinary product-analysis baseline.
Same-model peer agreement is not independent validation.

decision_blocked.statement: Should Truth → Perception → Action → Ownership → Effect be adopted as the working diagnostic framework for product reasoning in Decision Lab, and if so in what exact structural form; or should it be adapted/rejected before it influences future audits, UX decisions, or product instrumentation?
decision_blocked.current_default: Do not canonize the five-part framework yet. Use it only as a provisional heuristic until its constructs, topology, omissions, and discrimination value have been challenged against at least one strong alternative and a small set of real cases.
decision_blocked.reversal_condition: Promote or adapt the framework only if analysis shows that its components map to distinct failure mechanisms with different corrective actions/evidence needs, that fatal overlaps/omissions are either resolved or explicitly modeled, and that a minimal comparison can test whether it improves diagnosis beyond an ordinary unstructured product review.

signals: Truth and Effect look like endpoint validity questions, while Perception, Action and Ownership may be mediating mechanisms; this may mean the five items are not the same ontological type.

The deeper chain Reality → Model → Representation → Interpretation → Action → Learning may be more structurally coherent than the five questions, suggesting the five are projections or audit lenses rather than stages.
Perception may itself contain comprehension, trust, salience, interpretation and perceived value; one label may hide several materially different mechanisms.
Action may conflate knowing the next action with choosing it, initiating it, completing it and paying its cost.
Ownership may explain transfer in Decision Lab but may be irrelevant to products whose telos is one-shot execution, implying it could be conditional rather than universal.
Effect may be recursively fed back into Truth because observed effects update the system's model; a linear chain may miss the closed loop.
Motivation was excluded as a primitive on the theory that it is an outcome of other mechanisms, but this is not established; expected payoff or effort may be independent bottlenecks.

A competing formulation could be a fault tree or layered model such as Epistemic Validity → Representation Fidelity → Decision/Action Affordance → Internalization/Transfer → Outcome, with moderators such as motivation/trust/cost rather than a flat list.
The practical value criterion is not elegance. If two frameworks produce the same diagnosis and next move on the same cases, the extra framework has Δ0.
